1. Measure lantana in the same fixed plots each time.
What: presence, percent cover, stem count, and number of cut-stump resprouts.
Where: the plant community plots are the best starting unit.
How often: before weeding, then at the same interval after weeding each round.
Method: repeat the same plot boundaries and same counting rule every visit.

2. Measure shade in those same plots on the same dates.
What: canopy cover and, if possible, canopy openness.
Where: above each lantana plot, not in a nearby stand.
How often: every lantana visit.
Method: use one standard canopy method throughout, so the values are comparable.

What: tree height, basal area, and DBH, meaning stem diameter.
Where: the same plots.
How often: at least once at baseline, then after major canopy change.
Method: keep the plant community plot method so shade can be separated from stand structure.

What: whether the plot was weeded, when, how much was removed, and any fire, grazing, or cutting after that.
Where: each plot.
How often: every intervention and every revisit.
Method: one field sheet per plot, because without treatment history you cannot say shade caused the change.

5. Measure recruitment pressure.
What: new seedlings and nearby fruiting lantana.
Where: inside the plot and a short buffer around it.
How often: each revisit.
Method: count them separately from old stems, because comeback can be from resprouting or new germination.

turns.answer:
<!-- idli-result:{"result_id":"result-89d2dddce1628d3986a9dbd3"} -->

From the data this site has, the current surveys give recorded pairs, not demonstrated seed movement. The site’s own method notes show stronger inference needs repeated detections and tighter inputs than these pair tables have. So to turn a pair into real dispersal evidence next season, your team has to follow the animal, the fruit. The seed fate in the same watch, not just note that the bird was on the tree. These method notes are design notes from the site’s method catalogue, not fitted results.

1. Record the exact tree individual watched.
Where: every focal fruiting tree.
How often: every watch.
Method: tag the tree, note species, fruiting stage, crop size, and location.

2. Record the visitor identity and visit time.
Where: at the same focal tree.
How often: every visit during each watch.
Method: note animal species, start time, end time, visit length, and number of feeding events.

3. Record what the animal actually did with the fruit.
Where: at the fruiting crown or below it.
How often: every feeding event.
Method: separate swallowed, pecked, dropped, carried away, pulp-eaten, and seed-crushed.

4. Record whether the seed left the parent tree.
Where: under the crown and along the animal’s departure line when visible.
How often: every feeding event where handling is seen.
Method: note dropped under crown, carried away, or swallowed and flown off.

5. Record the number of seeds handled per visit.
Where: same focal watch.
How often: every visit.
Method: count fruits taken and seeds dropped or rejected.

6. Record deposition evidence away from the parent.
Where: fixed searches or seed traps under perches, roosts, fence lines, and likely fly-out routes.
How often: daily or every 2–3 days through fruiting.
Method: collect fresh droppings, spat seeds, and dropped fruits, linked back to the focal tree species where possible.

7. Record seed fate after deposition.
Where: beneath focal trees and at away-from-parent deposition points.
How often: revisit marked seeds through the season.
Method: mark seeds and note intact, germinated, predated, removed, dead, or seedling established.

8. Record distance from parent tree.
Where: every dropped, spat, or trap-caught seed.
How often: every seed event you can locate.
Method: measure distance band or exact distance so you can separate mere feeding from dispersal.

9. Record repeat watches on the same tree species across sites.
Where: degraded fragments, restored plots, and benchmark forest.
How often: multiple days per tree species and multiple trees per species.
Method: keep watch effort standard, so low records do not just mean low watching.

10. Record absences during standard watches.
Where: every focal tree watch.
How often: every watch.
Method: note full watch length even when no visitor comes, because repeat non-detections are needed to separate true scarcity from poor coverage.
